passage: By the third week in the girls' hostel, Disha no longer said she liked sleeping at eleven. At one in the morning the common room was full of instant noodles and a debate about whether the warden was a tyrant. Nirmala was the loudest, and everyone agreed. Disha nodded along, though she thought the warden had been fair over the water shortage. Two girls, Kavya and Sonal, drifted off to bed, and nobody remarked on it. Disha yawned into her sleeve, said "True, true," and stayed until three. In the mirror next morning, someone she barely knew looked back, with the hostel's opinions and her own dark circles.

qa.q: What were the girls debating in the common room?
qa.a: The girls were debating whether the warden was a tyrant.

qa.q: Why did Disha say "True, true" when she thought the warden had been fair?
qa.a: Disha wanted to fit in with the group and did not want to be the odd one; the barely known face in the mirror suggests a faint unease about losing herself.

qa.q: What small choice could Disha make the next night to keep both belonging and her own view?
qa.a: Disha could go to bed at her usual time like Kavya and Sonal did, and say one honest, mild sentence about the water shortage.

qa.q: How might Kavya or Sonal have seen leaving early for bed?
qa.a: Kavya and Sonal seem to have gone without needing an explanation, so leaving quietly may have felt fine to them; it shows the norm had a little room.

grounding: A new college student drifts into hostel habits of late nights and shared opinions, with the peer group becoming a mirror for identity.

passage: Dear Salma, the hostel here is bigger than our whole street. I have started staying up till two with the second-year girls in the corridor, which I never did at home. Last Saturday some of them slipped out for drinks. I said no the first time, but now I say "maybe next week" because saying no again feels like a wall. I laugh at jokes about people from our town that I would not have laughed at before. You once told me I always know what I think. Now I check the corridor first. I am not unhappy, just curious who I am becoming. Write soon. — Farida

qa.q: Until what time has Farida been staying up in the corridor?
qa.a: Farida has been staying up till two with the second-year girls in the corridor.

qa.q: Why does Farida say "maybe next week" instead of no again?
qa.a: Saying no again feels like a wall, so Farida is worried about being left out; the mix of curiosity and unease shows in the closing lines.

qa.q: What could Farida do next to check whether these new habits are really wanted?
qa.a: Farida could pause before answering the next invitation, write down what Farida actually wants, and talk it over with Salma or a trusted adult.

qa.q: What might Salma be thinking when reading that Farida now checks the corridor first?
qa.a: Salma may feel concerned and fond, since Salma once told Farida "I always know what I think", and might reply with a gentle check-in rather than a scolding.

grounding: A new hostel resident drifts into late nights and the group's habits, with the peer group becoming the main mirror away from family.
